## Light Interacting with Surfaces {#sec-light_interacting_with_surfaces}

Visible light is electromagnetic radiation, exhibiting wave effects like
diffraction. For many imaging models, however, it is helpful to
introduce the abstraction of a **light ray**, describing the light
radiation heading in a particular direction from a particular location
in space (@fig-lightSpray). A light ray is specified by its position, direction, and
intensity as a function of wavelength and polarization. In this
treatment, we ignore diffraction effects.

![A light ray from the sun strikes a surface and generates outgoing rays
of intensity and color depending on the angles of the incoming and
outgoing rays relative to the surface orientation.](figures/imaging/brdf.png){#fig-lightSpray width="75%"}

Let an incident light ray be from direction $\mathbf{p}$ and of power,
$\ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda)$, as a function of spectral wavelength $\lambda$ ().
The power of the outgoing light, reflected in the direction,
$\mathbf{q}$, is determined by what is called the **bidirectional
reflection distribution function** (BRDF), $F$, of the surface. If the
surface normal is $\mathbf{n}$, then outgoing power is some function,
$F$, of the surface normal, the incoming and outgoing ray directions,
the wavelength, and the incoming light power:
$$\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{n}, \lambda, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \right)
$$ {#eq-Lambert}

### Lambertian Surfaces

In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see @Matusik2002),
describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even
surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated
reflectance distributions @Oren1994. A useful approximation describing
diffuse reflection is the **Lambertian model**, with a particularly
simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity,
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the
incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface
reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right)  = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$${#eq-lambert}

where $a$ is the surface **reflectance**, or
**albedo**, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$
points toward the source of the incident light. Note that the brightness
of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface
relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the
surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light
is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a
function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.

interactions.label: Surface Type
interactions.teaches: Switches between a Lambertian surface (diffuse reflection, uniform in all directions) and a specular surface (glossy reflection, focused in a mirror-like lobe)

interactions.label: Incident Angle (θ)
interactions.teaches: Adjusting the angle of incidence changes the projected area of the beam, scaling the total reflected energy by the cosine of the angle (n · p)

demo_steps.title: Diffuse (Lambertian) reflection
demo_steps.narration: In a Lambertian surface, light scatters equally in all directions. The outgoing intensity is independent of the viewing direction q — the green spray forms a perfect hemisphere whose overall size is scaled only by the incoming light's angle.

demo_steps.title: The Cosine Law (n · p)
demo_steps.narration: Tilt the incoming light to a shallow angle of 75 degrees. Notice how the green reflection hemisphere shrinks. Because the incoming light is spread over a larger surface area, less energy is reflected per unit area, demonstrating the n · p relationship.

demo_steps.title: Specular lobe
demo_steps.narration: Switch to a glossy surface. The reflection is no longer uniform; instead, it concentrates into a specular lobe pointing in the mirror-reflection direction. The outgoing ray q is now brightest when it aligns with this lobe.

demo_steps.title: Grazing angle specular stretch
demo_steps.narration: At grazing angles, many real-world surfaces become highly specular. The lobe stretches and brightens along the surface boundary, showing why wet roads or polished tables look incredibly bright when viewed at low angles.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: Slightly elevated orthographic 3D view, looking down at the surface plane from the front-left to clearly separate the incoming ray (left) from the outgoing ray and reflection lobe (right).

(2) This broadside view means the camera is positioned looking primarily along the plane's longitudinal center, which corresponds to an azimuth of approximately -35 degrees (to see the perspective recession on both sides). (3) The plane is visible as a moderately thick parallelogram rather than a flat line, indicating a clear overhead elevation cue of around 25-30 degrees.

$$\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}}, \mathbf{n}, \lambda, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \right)
$$ {#eq-Lambert}

### Lambertian Surfaces

In general, BRDFs can be quite complicated (see @Matusik2002),
describing both diffuse and specular components of reflection. Even
surfaces with completely diffuse reflections can give complicated
reflectance distributions @Oren1994. A useful approximation describing
diffuse reflection is the **Lambertian model**, with a particularly
simple BRDF, which we denote as $F_L$. The outgoing ray intensity,
$\ell_{\texttt{out}}$, is a function only of the surface orientation relative to the
incoming and outgoing ray directions, the wavelength, a scalar surface
reflectance, and the incoming light power:
$$
\ell_{\texttt{out}} = F_{L} \left( \ell_{\texttt{in}} (\lambda), \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{p} \right)  = a \ell_{\texttt{in}}(\lambda) \left( \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p} \right),
$${#eq-lambert}

where $a$ is the surface **reflectance**, or
**albedo**, $\mathbf{n}$ is the surface normal vector, and $\mathbf{p}$
points toward the source of the incident light. Note that the brightness
of the outgoing light ray depends on the orientation of the surface
relative to the incident ray, as well as the reflectance, $a$, of the
surface. For a Lambertian surface, the intensity of the reflected light
is a function of the direction of the incoming light ray, but not a
function of the outgoing direction of the ray, $\mathbf{q}$.

interactions.label: Surface Type
interactions.teaches: Switches between a Lambertian surface (diffuse reflection, uniform in all directions) and a specular surface (glossy reflection, focused in a mirror-like lobe)

interactions.label: Incident Angle (θ)
interactions.teaches: Adjusting the angle of incidence changes the projected area of the beam, scaling the total reflected energy by the cosine of the angle (n · p)

demo_steps.title: Diffuse (Lambertian) reflection
demo_steps.narration: In a Lambertian surface, light scatters equally in all directions. The outgoing intensity is independent of the viewing direction q — the green spray forms a perfect hemisphere whose overall size is scaled only by the incoming light's angle.

demo_steps.title: The Cosine Law (n · p)
demo_steps.narration: Tilt the incoming light to a shallow angle of 75 degrees. Notice how the green reflection hemisphere shrinks. Because the incoming light is spread over a larger surface area, less energy is reflected per unit area, demonstrating the n · p relationship.

demo_steps.title: Specular lobe
demo_steps.narration: Switch to a glossy surface. The reflection is no longer uniform; instead, it concentrates into a specular lobe pointing in the mirror-reflection direction. The outgoing ray q is now brightest when it aligns with this lobe.

demo_steps.title: Grazing angle specular stretch
demo_steps.narration: At grazing angles, many real-world surfaces become highly specular. The lobe stretches and brightens along the surface boundary, showing why wet roads or polished tables look incredibly bright when viewed at low angles.

evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer implemented several highly functional and pedagogically rich interactions: (1) A dropdown selector ('Surface Type') to toggle between Lambertian (diffuse) and Specular (glossy) reflection models, which dynamically alters the 3D scattering spray geometry and outgoing ray scale. (2) An 'Incident Angle' slider that rotates the incoming light ray and 'p' vector group, dynamically updating the cosine-law scaling, the mirror-reflection lobe direction, and the relative scale of the outgoing ray. (3) 3D element hotspots using 'registerInteractive' which display informative tooltips/popups on click/hover for various vector elements. (4) A guided step-through demo framework with 4 distinct pedagogical states, complete with a custom tweening animation when transitioning angles.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: Core concepts: 1. BRDF (Bidirectional Reflection Distribution Function) characterizing surface reflectance; 2. Lambertian reflectance depending on the cosine of the incident angle (n · p) and scattering uniformly in all directions; 3. Specular reflectance focusing light into a lobe around the mirror reflection direction. All concepts are accurately represented in the interactive scene: changing the incident angle correctly scales the diffuse hemisphere according to the cosine law, and switching to specular mode shifts the scattering into a directional lobe where the intensity along the viewer ray 'q' is mathematically linked to its alignment with the specular reflection direction.
evaluation.notes: The implementation is of outstanding quality, achieving perfect scores in both concept accuracy and interactivity. It flawlessly demonstrates BRDF principles with dynamic Lambertian/Specular toggling, real-time cosine-law scaling, and an engaging guided step-through tutorial.
